Senses.Explanation: To hit the bench or platform-seat used during an address to the assembly. The strike is public teaching-hall conduct, not merely damage to furniture: it often supplies the last percussive event before leaving the seat, but it can also become a turn in an exchange. Yuanwu Keqin raises the whisk and asks whether the assembly sees, then strikes the teaching seat and asks again. Foyin Qing makes the contrast explicit by asking whether they see the raised whisk and whether they hear the struck seat. Dahui Zonggao labels the raised whisk “form” and the seat-strike “sound.” Shishuang Chuyuan strikes once with his staff, asks whether the assembly understands, and cites the line “one strike, and what was known was forgotten.” Dayu Shouzhi answers a six-rung-reviewed unnamed questioner's question about buddha by striking once and saying it has already been forgotten. Songyuan Chongyue strikes once with the whisk and asks whether his listeners feel pain or an itch. The omitted or named instrument and the various questions change the use, not the physical action. The phrase has 686 matches in 141 texts.

Senses.Explanation: Zen masters repeatedly use this recurring lament as a capping line: ‘On the coral pillow, two tracks of tears—half from missing you, half from resenting you.’ Yongji Rong asks whether he is pleased with the visiting Chan master who urged him to teach the assembly or annoyed with him, pauses, and answers with the couplet. Shaweng Huihai refuses both one-sided condemnation and one-sided praise of the awakened Buddha, then gives the same line. Fogu Xingwen raises the National Teacher's ‘I thought I had failed you, but you have failed me,’ asks how ‘failing me / failing you’ is to be understood, and caps it with the couplet. Guting Shanjian applies it after saying that Dongshan exposed Xuefeng completely although Xuefeng later inherited from Deshan Xuanjian; Hanyu Hongxian and Huijue Yi use it while mourning their teachers, Zixian Jue and Poshan Haiming. Elsewhere Baiyun Shouduan strikes his staff, asks whether the assembly understands, gives the line, and leaves the seat, while Xiangya Xingting uses it when his assembly cannot answer a tea test. These cases establish a line that keeps longing, attachment, remembrance, or gratitude together with grievance or resentment and repeatedly resists a one-sided praise-or-blame verdict. Mourning and public tests are settings in which masters use it, not additional senses. The coral pillow supplies the scene; these passages do not make coral itself a Zen symbol.

Senses.Explanation: Jeweled towers and jade halls are the palace-image in Baiyun Shouduan's blade-of-grass saying: the palace appears on one grass blade, yet the same blade can cover it. Baiyun Shouduan frames both directions around whether one has truly sweated once. Qianyan Yuanzhang asks how a doubtful listener could make a grass blade into a great body, establish a monastery, or show the palace on it; Feiyin Tongrong recasts the same reversal as making a palace from grass. Senses.Explanation: To draw the bow after the thief has passed is to act only after the decisive moment has already gone. Xuedou Chongxian applies the line after Zhaozhou's exchange with Huangbo and laughs at the belated move. Yuanwu Keqin gives it as an answer to a follow-up that arrives after the point; Ying'an Tanhua, Yuejiang Zhengyin, Liao'an Qingyu, and Tianyin Yuanxiu likewise use it to mark commentary or rescue that comes too late. The Chan bend is temporal and procedural: a response may be sharp in itself yet miss because the live encounter has already passed.
